Area.evidence_source: Many men idealized self-management strategies to independently overcome their suicidality wherein self-reliance was mobilized in response to both broad taboos around mental illness and the normative dimensions of gender identities. Here, we were interested in placing these dynamics within the layers of isolation and suicidality (including families, work, and formalized care) and to position ineffectual and self-harming management within these broader milieus. The attempts to restore their mental health with ineffectual and self-harming management strategies were evident in a variety of isolating practices that centered on men concealing mental illness from others and/or distracting themselves (and others) from their suicidality. Ineffectual self-care contributed to men's isolation, often manifesting in the form of self-harming management. Predominant among these was substance use, a normative masculine recreation and resolution used to both brighten and blunt feelings. These practices, however, wielded self-harm, exacerbating the men's isolation and suicidality, while comprehensively failing to address the issues driving those self-destructive behaviors.
